bad.code: Save

good.code: <button type="button" onClick={handleSave}>Save</button>

rules.rationale: Native semantics provide keyboard behavior, accessibility information, and browser interoperability with less custom code.
rules.summary: Use the native element whose semantics match the interaction or content before recreating that behavior with generic elements.
rules.title: Prefer semantic HTML

bad.code: Menu

good.code:
<button type="button" onClick={openMenu}>
  Menu
</button>

rules.rationale: Pointer-only controls exclude keyboard and many assistive-technology users and usually indicate missing native semantics.
rules.summary: Every interactive operation available with a pointer must also be operable from the keyboard when the platform interaction supports it.
rules.title: Keyboard access is mandatory

rules.rationale: Keyboard users need a persistent visual indicator of where the next interaction will occur.
rules.summary: Interactive elements must expose a clear visible state when they receive keyboard focus.
rules.title: Keep focus visible

bad.code:
<button type="button" onClick={closeDialog}>
  <CloseIcon />
</button>

good.code:
<button
  type="button"
  aria-label="Close dialog"
  onClick={closeDialog}
>
  <CloseIcon aria-hidden="true" />
</button>

rules.rationale: A control that is visually recognizable but unnamed programmatically is ambiguous or unusable to assistive technology.
rules.summary: Inputs and interactive controls must expose a meaningful programmatic name through visible text, a label, or appropriate accessible naming.
rules.title: Controls need accessible names

bad.code: ●

good.code: {isOverdue ? "Overdue" : "On time"}

rules.rationale: Color perception varies and may be unavailable entirely. Redundant cues make meaning robust for more users and environments.
rules.summary: When color carries status or meaning, provide another perceivable cue such as text, iconography, shape, or position.
rules.title: Do not communicate with color alone

rules.rationale: Motion can cause discomfort or make interfaces harder to use, and operating systems expose a preference specifically for this need.
rules.summary: Non-essential animation and smooth motion should adapt when the user requests reduced motion.
rules.title: Respect reduced motion preferences

good.code:
// Reuse the project's established boundary.
const users = await userRepository.list();

rules.rationale: Agents can create parallel architectures and duplicate helpers when they optimize only for the local prompt.
rules.summary: AI output should use established project patterns before introducing new abstractions.
rules.title: Generated code follows existing architecture

good.code:
// The legacy endpoint can return stale data for ~30s after account merges.
const user = await userApi.get(id);

rules.rationale: Generated narration adds noise quickly and creates stale text maintainers must keep synchronized.
rules.summary: Remove AI comments that merely narrate the code.
rules.title: Generated comments must add context

bad.code:
Requested: Fix invoice rounding

Generated diff:
- Fix invoice rounding
- Rename money utilities
- Move billing folders
- Reformat unrelated tests

good.code:
Requested: Fix invoice rounding

Generated diff:
- Fix invoice rounding
- Add the regression test

rules.rationale: Small coherent diffs are easier to validate, review, revert, and debug.
rules.summary: Do not expand generated changes into unrelated cleanup or speculative refactors.
rules.title: Change the smallest coherent surface

good.code:
import { formatCurrency } from "@/shared/currency";

const label = formatCurrency(total);

rules.rationale: Agents can generate locally correct duplicates because they do not automatically share a human maintainer's memory of the codebase.
rules.summary: Before generating a new helper, component, type, dependency, or pattern, search for an existing solution in the project.
rules.title: Inspect before creating

rules.rationale: Plausible-looking hallucinated APIs are especially expensive because generated code can appear correct until build or runtime.
rules.summary: Do not invent package exports, framework behavior, command flags, or platform capabilities from memory when they can be verified.
rules.title: Verify external APIs

rules.rationale: Speculative edge cases bloat types, branches, and tests while obscuring the conditions the system genuinely needs to handle.
rules.summary: Generated defensive code and tests should reflect actual contracts, trust boundaries, and realistic failure modes.
rules.title: Do not invent impossible edge cases

bad.code:
# Generated files look plausible, so stop here.
git status

good.code:
pnpm typecheck
pnpm lint
pnpm test
pnpm build

rules.rationale: AI can produce syntactically plausible changes that fail existing contracts elsewhere in the repository.
rules.summary: Generated changes are not complete until the relevant type, lint, test, build, and project-specific validation commands have been run.
rules.title: Run the project's checks

bad.code:
// Product has sku, but no id/_id.
const cache = new InMemoryCache();

rules.rationale: Apollo's normalized cache can only merge references to the same entity reliably when it can identify that entity consistently across operations.
rules.summary: Ensure normalized entity types have stable identifiers, configuring keyFields when the schema does not use Apollo's default ID conventions.
rules.title: Define stable cache identity

good.note: Choose a policy per freshness requirement; this is one example, not a universal default.

rules.rationale: Fetch policy is a correctness and UX decision: it controls whether the UI trusts cached data, waits for the network, or persists results for future consumers.
rules.summary: Use cache-first, cache-and-network, network-only, no-cache, and related policies according to data freshness requirements rather than applying one policy everywhere.
rules.title: Choose fetch policies deliberately

rules.rationale: Apollo can normalize returned entities automatically, reducing manual cache manipulation and extra network requests.
rules.summary: When practical, mutation responses should include the modified entities and fields the UI/cache needs to reconcile.
rules.title: Return modified entities from mutations

bad.code:
await deleteTodo({ variables: { id } });
// GET_TODOS may still contain the deleted item.

rules.rationale: Server mutation success does not automatically guarantee every cached list or derived field reflects the new server state.
rules.summary: After a mutation, rely on normalized returned entities, update the cache, or selectively refetch affected queries instead of leaving stale client state.
rules.title: Reconcile mutation results explicitly

bad.code:
const nextPage = await fetchMore({ variables: { offset: items.length } });
setItems((items) => [...items, ...nextPage.data.feed]);

rules.rationale: Field policies centralize how the normalized cache reads and merges a field, producing consistent behavior for every consumer.
rules.summary: When cached fields require argument-aware identity, pagination, or custom merging, define that behavior in typePolicies instead of scattering cache repair logic across components.
rules.title: Encode pagination and merge semantics in field policies

rules.rationale: A GraphQL response may contain both data and errors; treating every failure as identical can discard useful data or display invalid partial state.
rules.summary: Choose errorPolicy based on whether partial data is usable and distinguish GraphQL execution errors from network or transport failures.
rules.title: Handle GraphQL errors and partial data intentionally

rules.rationale: Separating responsibilities makes code easier to reason about, test, replace, and review without requiring knowledge of unrelated behavior.
rules.summary: Rendering, orchestration, transformation, persistence, and external I/O should have explicit ownership.
rules.title: Separate responsibilities

rules.rationale: Explicit dependencies expose coupling and make ownership, testing, and replacement easier to understand.
rules.summary: A module should receive or import the dependencies it actually uses rather than reaching through unrelated layers.
rules.title: Keep dependencies explicit

bad.code:
saveEntity("article", article, { draft: true, audit: false });
saveEntity("invoice", invoice, { draft: false, audit: true });

rules.rationale: Small duplication is cheaper than a premature abstraction that couples unrelated use cases and becomes difficult to change.
rules.summary: Do not create a shared abstraction until the repeated behavior and its stable differences are understood.
rules.title: Abstract after understanding repetition

rules.rationale: Isolated side effects make behavior easier to test, replay, reason about, and replace.
rules.summary: Prefer pure transformation logic internally and isolate network, storage, clock, DOM, and other side effects behind clear boundaries.
rules.title: Keep side effects at boundaries

good.code:
const [items, setItems] = useState<Item[]>([]);
const itemCount = items.length;

rules.rationale: Duplicated state can drift. A canonical owner with derived views removes synchronization bugs and clarifies responsibility.
rules.summary: Do not maintain multiple independently writable representations of the same fact.
rules.title: Keep one source of truth

exceptions: A deliberate compatibility boundary or public facade may justify forwarding when it protects consumers from an unstable implementation.

good.code: await fetch("/api/users");

rules.rationale: Pass-through layers add files and indirection without reducing coupling or complexity.
rules.summary: An abstraction should add meaning, policy, transformation, or a stable boundary rather than merely forward every call unchanged.
rules.title: Do not add pass-through abstractions

bad.code:
src/
  components/
    OrderList.tsx
    UserAvatar.tsx
  hooks/
    useOrders.ts
    useProfile.ts
  services/
    orders.ts
    profile.ts

good.code:
src/
  orders/
    OrderList.tsx
    useOrders.ts
    orderApi.ts
  profile/
    UserAvatar.tsx
    useProfile.ts
    profileApi.ts

rules.rationale: Domain-oriented structure keeps behavior that changes together physically close and makes ownership easier to discover.
rules.summary: Prefer module boundaries that reflect product or business concepts over generic buckets that accumulate unrelated code.
rules.title: Organize around cohesive domains

bad.code: return users.filter((u) => u.a && !u.s).map((u) => u.e);

rules.rationale: Code is maintained and reviewed far more often than it is initially written. Readability lowers review cost, defect risk, and onboarding time.
rules.summary: Prefer code that communicates intent without requiring reconstruction by the reader.
rules.title: Optimize for understanding

bad.code: strategies.filter((s) => s.goalType);

exceptions: Established mathematical notation in a clearly mathematical scope.
Conventional short names whose meaning is unambiguous in the immediate context.

good.code: strategies.filter((strategy) => strategy.goalType);

rules.rationale: Descriptive names reduce the surrounding code a reader must inspect to understand behavior.
rules.summary: Names should communicate the role of a value, function, or module.
rules.title: Use descriptive names

bad.code: let user = getUser();

good.code: const user = getUser();

rules.rationale: Stable bindings reduce the number of state transitions a reader must track and prevent accidental reassignment.
rules.summary: Declare bindings with const unless reassignment is required.
rules.title: Prefer const

bad.code:
// Filter active users
const activeUsers = users.filter((user) => user.active);

good.code:
// Suspended accounts remain for audit history, so exclude only inactive accounts.
const activeUsers = users.filter((user) => user.active);

rules.rationale: Narrative comments duplicate code and become stale. Decision comments preserve context the implementation cannot express.
rules.summary: Do not narrate obvious code. Document decisions, constraints, and workarounds.
rules.title: Comments explain why

good.code:
export const calculateTax = (total: number) =>
  taxService.calculate(total);

rules.rationale: Dead code expands the surface maintainers must understand, obscures what is still supported, and creates false confidence that obsolete paths are tested.
rules.summary: Remove unused functions, imports, exports, files, branches, and dependencies when their last real use disappears.
rules.title: Delete dead code

bad.code: if (attempts >= 5) lockAccount();

exceptions: Values whose meaning is inherent to the operation, such as 0 when checking an array length.

good.code:
const MAX_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS = 5;

if (attempts >= MAX_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS) lockAccount();

rules.rationale: A named value communicates why a number or string exists and makes policy changes less error-prone.
rules.summary: Give unexplained values a name when their meaning, policy, or unit is not obvious from local context.
rules.title: Name meaningful constants

rules.rationale: Excessive fragmentation forces readers to jump between files to understand one behavior and can be as harmful as oversized modules.
rules.summary: Place closely related logic together instead of scattering tiny pieces across unnecessary files.
rules.title: Keep cohesive code together

exceptions: Do not introduce multiple early exits when they make cleanup or transactional behavior harder to reason about.

good.code:
if (!user || !user.active) return;

save(user);

rules.rationale: Deep nesting increases the amount of state a reader must hold in mind. Early exits can make the successful path visually obvious.
rules.summary: Prefer guard clauses and early exits when they make the main control flow easier to follow.
rules.title: Reduce nesting when it improves clarity

bad.code:
const MAX_PAYMENT_RETRIES = 2;

export const retryPayment = () => { /* ... */ };

rules.rationale: Refactors should change structure without silently deleting historical context that future maintainers still need.
rules.summary: When moving code, preserve explanations and constraints that remain relevant to the behavior.
rules.title: Preserve non-obvious context during refactors

rules.rationale: Every export becomes a dependency point that constrains future refactoring and increases the surface maintainers must understand.
rules.summary: Do not export functions, types, modules, or abstractions that have no external consumer.
rules.title: Keep the public surface minimal

rules.rationale: Hoisting communicates independence, avoids needless recreation, and makes the helper easier to test or reuse locally.
rules.summary: If a helper does not depend on its parent function's local values, define it in a stable outer scope.
rules.title: Hoist context-free helpers

bad.code: .redBox {}

good.code: .errorMessage {}

rules.rationale: Role-based names survive visual redesigns and communicate intent without coupling markup to presentation.
rules.summary: Class names should describe what an element is responsible for rather than its current visual treatment.
rules.title: Name styles by role, not appearance

exceptions: A truly one-off value may stay local when promoting it would create a meaningless token.
rules.rationale: Tokens keep visual decisions consistent and make system-wide changes possible without hunting through feature styles.
rules.summary: Repeated semantic values such as colors, spacing, radii, typography, and elevation should come from a shared token source.
rules.title: Use tokens for shared visual decisions

rules.rationale: Layout primitives encode relationships and adapt to content, while manual nudges are brittle across font sizes, translations, and responsive states.
rules.summary: Use flexbox, grid, intrinsic sizing, and normal flow before offsets or spacer elements used only to force alignment.
rules.title: Prefer layout systems over manual nudges

rules.rationale: Global leakage creates hidden coupling where changing one feature unexpectedly changes another.
rules.summary: Component-specific styling should not leak into unrelated parts of the application through broad global selectors.
rules.title: Keep component styles scoped

bad.code:
import uniq from "lodash/uniq";

const uniqueIds = uniq(ids);

good.code: const uniqueIds = [...new Set(ids)];

rules.rationale: Every dependency adds bundle, security, upgrade, compatibility, and maintenance cost that native capabilities do not.
rules.summary: Check whether the language, runtime, browser, or existing stack already solves the problem before adding a package.
rules.title: Prefer the platform before a dependency

good.code: const shouldAlternate = index % 2 !== 0;

rules.rationale: Convenient packages can become long-lived architectural commitments after their original use case disappears.
rules.summary: A runtime dependency should provide enough durable value to outweigh its bundle size, API surface, security surface, and upgrade cost.
rules.title: Justify runtime dependencies

rules.rationale: Unused packages continue to consume install time, security attention, and upgrade effort while providing no value.
rules.summary: Delete packages when no production, test, build, or tooling path still requires them.
rules.title: Remove unused dependencies

rules.rationale: Multiple libraries for the same job increase bundle size, cognitive load, inconsistent conventions, and migration cost.
rules.summary: Do not introduce a second library for a capability the project already solves adequately.
rules.title: Avoid duplicate solutions

rules.rationale: Flags are temporary branches in production code. Without an explicit end condition they become permanent complexity.
rules.summary: Create flags with an owner and a planned condition or date for removal.
rules.title: Every feature flag needs a removal plan

good.code: return renderNewCheckout();

rules.rationale: Completed flags create dead branches and make maintainers reason about product states that can no longer occur.
rules.summary: When rollout is complete, remove the code branches, tests that exist only for the flag, and the remote flag definition.
rules.title: Delete flags after rollout

rules.rationale: Scattered flag checks create combinatorial states and make eventual removal much harder.
rules.summary: Evaluate a feature flag in as few places as practical and pass the resulting behavior or state inward.
rules.title: Keep flag decisions at clear boundaries

rules.rationale: A flag creates multiple production paths; only testing the preferred path leaves the fallback branch to rot.
rules.summary: While a feature flag is active, test the meaningful enabled and disabled behavior that can reach production.
rules.title: Test both reachable flag states

rules.rationale: Operation names make logs, traces, errors, persisted operations, and refetch behavior easier to identify than anonymous documents.
rules.summary: Give queries, mutations, and subscriptions unique meaningful operation names.
rules.title: Name production operations

rules.rationale: Variables preserve a stable operation document, keep values typed separately, and avoid fragile or unsafe string construction.
rules.summary: Use GraphQL variables for runtime values instead of interpolating user or application data into operation strings.
rules.title: Pass dynamic values as variables

rules.rationale: Fragments keep repeated data requirements consistent and make component-level GraphQL requirements composable.
rules.summary: Extract repeated or component-owned field groups into named fragments rather than duplicating the same selection in many operations.
rules.title: Use fragments for genuinely shared selection sets

bad.code:
pnpm type-check
# GraphQL documents are never checked against the schema

good.code:
pnpm graphql:validate
pnpm type-check
good.note: Use schema-aware validation or code generation in CI; the exact command depends on the project toolchain.

rules.rationale: GraphQL's schema can prove invalid fields, selections, and variable types before runtime, making schema-aware validation one of its strongest safety features.
rules.summary: Generate or check client operations against the current schema instead of relying on hand-maintained assumptions about fields and types.
rules.title: Validate operations against the schema

bad.code:
// Schema: nickname: String
type User = { nickname: string };

good.code:
// Schema: nickname: String
type User = { nickname: string | null };

rules.rationale: GraphQL nullability expresses real response and input guarantees; weakening or strengthening it locally creates impossible assumptions.
rules.summary: Model nullable fields and variables exactly as the schema declares them rather than erasing nullability in client types.
rules.title: Treat nullability as part of the contract

rules.rationale: Unbounded lists create unpredictable latency, payload size, memory pressure, and rendering cost.
rules.summary: Do not design clients or schemas around fetching an ever-growing collection in one operation; use an appropriate pagination model.
rules.title: Paginate collections that can grow without bound

bad.code: <button type="button">Save changes</button>

good.code:
<button type="button">
  {t("actions.saveChanges")}
</button>

rules.rationale: Hardcoded interface strings create inaccessible translation boundaries and are expensive to find after a product expands to more locales.
rules.summary: Labels, messages, placeholders, tooltips, empty states, and other user-visible copy should come from the application's localization system.
rules.title: Localize user-visible text

bad.code: const message = "You have " + count + (count === 1 ? " item" : " items");

rules.rationale: Word order, plural rules, gender, and punctuation vary by language; concatenation assumes English-like grammar.
rules.summary: Use the localization system's placeholders and plural/select features rather than assembling human sentences from fragments.
rules.title: Parameterize messages instead of concatenating sentences

bad.code: const label = `${date.getMonth() + 1}/${date.getDate()}/${date.getFullYear()}`;

rules.rationale: Intl encodes locale-specific formatting rules and avoids shipping another library for capabilities already provided by the platform.
rules.summary: Prefer Intl.DateTimeFormat, Intl.NumberFormat, and related platform APIs for dates, numbers, currencies, lists, and relative time.
rules.title: Use Intl for locale-sensitive formatting

rules.rationale: Translated labels can grow substantially, and RTL locales invert directional relationships that fixed-width or left/right-specific layouts may encode incorrectly.
rules.summary: Avoid UI assumptions that only hold for short English text or left-to-right content.
rules.title: Design layouts for text expansion and direction

rules.rationale: async changes the function's return contract and error behavior. Adding it without Promise semantics misleads callers and readers.
rules.summary: Do not mark a function async unless it awaits work or intentionally exposes a Promise-returning contract.
rules.title: Use async only for Promise semantics

bad.code: const city = user && user.address && user.address.city;

good.code: const city = user?.address?.city;

rules.rationale: Correct optional chaining makes uncertainty explicit. Defensive chaining on guaranteed values hides incorrect types and weakens reasoning.
rules.summary: Prefer optional chaining when a value may legitimately be nullish, and avoid it when the contract guarantees the value exists.
rules.title: Use optional chaining for genuine nullish access

rules.rationale: Default parameters centralize input normalization and avoid mutation or guard boilerplate inside the function body.
rules.summary: When undefined should map to a stable default, express that contract in the function signature.
rules.title: Prefer default parameters for default inputs

bad.code:
parseInt(value);
obj.hasOwnProperty(key);

good.code:
Number.parseInt(value, 10);
Object.hasOwn(obj, key);

rules.rationale: Namespaced APIs communicate intent and avoid historical coercion or prototype pitfalls.
rules.summary: Use Number.parseInt, Number.isNaN, Object.hasOwn, and other precise modern built-ins instead of ambiguous legacy globals.
rules.title: Prefer namespace-safe built-ins

rules.rationale: A narrow catch boundary makes it clear what failed and prevents unrelated programming errors from being mistaken for expected operational failures.
rules.summary: Keep setup and unrelated transformation outside a try block unless those operations are intentionally part of the same failure boundary.
rules.title: Scope try/catch to the operation that can fail

bad.code: const sortedUsers = users.sort(compareUsers);

good.code: const sortedUsers = users.toSorted(compareUsers);

rules.rationale: Non-mutating operations make ownership explicit and prevent changes from leaking through shared references.
rules.summary: Use APIs such as toSorted, toReversed, and toSpliced when callers should retain the original collection.
rules.title: Prefer non-mutating collection APIs when mutation is not intended

bad.code: createReport(data, true, 50, false, "USD");

good.code: createReport({ data, currency: "USD", includeDrafts: true, limit: 50 });

rules.rationale: Named arguments make call sites self-documenting and allow the API to evolve without argument-order traps.
rules.summary: When a function has several same-shaped or optional arguments, prefer one named options object over a long positional signature.
rules.title: Use an options object when positional parameters stop being obvious

bad.code:
const Component = observer(() =>
{store$.name.get()}
);

rules.rationale: Legend-State v3 recommends useValue for React Compiler compatibility because Hook calls remain visible to the compiler while arbitrary get() calls may be memoized.
rules.summary: In new React code, read observables reactively through useValue instead of relying on observer plus get() tracking.
rules.title: Use useValue for React subscriptions

bad.code:
const userId = session$.userId.get();
analytics.track("checkout", { userId });

good.code:
const userId = session$.userId.peek();
analytics.track("checkout", { userId });
good.note: peek() makes the intentional non-reactive read explicit.

rules.rationale: get() participates in Legend-State dependency tracking while peek() explicitly opts out, so the choice communicates reactivity intent.
rules.summary: Use get() in tracking contexts when changes should be observed and peek() when the read deliberately must not subscribe.
rules.title: Use peek only when non-reactive access is intentional

good.code: store$.profile.name.set("Ada");

rules.rationale: Mutating raw data bypasses Legend-State notifications, and setting the same reference back may produce no observable change.
rules.summary: Do not mutate raw objects returned from an observable and then set the same reference back; update the observable node with set, assign, or another notifying API.
rules.title: Update observable state through observable APIs

bad.code:
store$.data.set(response.data);
store$.isLoading.set(false);

rules.rationale: assign batches its individual writes so observers update once and the operation is represented as one coherent state transition.
rules.summary: When several sibling fields change as one logical operation, prefer assign over a sequence of independent set calls.
rules.title: Batch sibling updates with assign

bad.code:
const state = useValue(store$);
return <Badge>{state.notifications.unread}</Badge>;

good.code:
const unread = useValue(store$.notifications.unread);
return <Badge>{unread}</Badge>;

rules.rationale: Legend-State's performance model depends on minimizing tracked observables so unrelated changes do not rerender parent components.
rules.summary: Prefer fine-grained subscriptions or computed useValue selectors over reading broad trees when only a small value drives rendering.
rules.title: Subscribe at the narrowest useful observable

exceptions: Purely in-memory observables that never cross a serialization boundary may intentionally contain functions or other supported runtime values.

good.note: Use plain values for observable nodes that are persisted, synchronized, or transported.

rules.rationale: Legend-State itself can hold functions and rich values, but serialization layers cannot reliably preserve arbitrary runtime objects or circular references.
rules.summary: When observable data crosses persistence, transport, devtool, or application-specific serialization boundaries, keep that state plain and serializable.
rules.title: Keep persisted or synchronized state serializable

rules.rationale: Server Components reduce client JavaScript and can fetch data close to its source without exposing server credentials.
rules.summary: In the App Router, keep components server-side unless they require state, event handlers, effects, custom client hooks, or browser-only APIs.
rules.title: Default to Server Components

rules.rationale: Everything imported below a use client boundary contributes to the client graph, so unnecessarily high boundaries increase shipped JavaScript.
rules.summary: Mark the client entry point that needs interactivity instead of moving an entire page or layout into the client module graph.
rules.title: Keep use client boundaries as small as practical

good.code:
// Server Component
return <ClientPrice amount={12} currency="USD" />;
good.note: Pass serializable data and keep ordinary client behavior inside the Client Component.

rules.rationale: The React Server Component payload crosses a network boundary and cannot transport arbitrary runtime values such as callbacks.
rules.summary: Values passed from Server Components into Client Component entry points must be serializable by React.
rules.title: Pass serializable props across the server-client boundary

bad.code:
export const getUsers = () => db.user.findMany();
export const apiSecret = process.env.API_SECRET;

good.code:
import "server-only";

export const getUsers = () => db.user.findMany();

rules.rationale: Shared JavaScript module graphs make accidental environment leakage possible; build-time server-only guards turn that mistake into an explicit error.
rules.summary: Keep secrets, privileged data access, and server-only modules behind server boundaries and mark them server-only when accidental client import is plausible.
rules.title: Protect server-only code from client imports

rules.rationale: Calling your own server endpoint from a Server Component adds an unnecessary network hop and duplicates a boundary that is already local.
rules.summary: When code already runs on the server, call the data source or shared server data function directly instead of making an HTTP request to your own Route Handler.
rules.title: Fetch server data directly from Server Components

bad.code:
const user = await getUser();
const posts = await getPosts();

rules.rationale: Sequential independent requests accumulate latency, while parallel fetching and streaming can deliver useful UI earlier.
rules.summary: Start independent server requests in parallel and use Suspense/streaming boundaries when slow work should not block the whole route.
rules.title: Avoid avoidable data-fetching waterfalls

rules.rationale: Premature micro-optimization obscures code, while repeated work over genuinely large datasets creates measurable cost.
rules.summary: Prefer readability by default; reduce passes and allocations when scale makes the cost meaningful.
rules.title: Optimize where scale exists

bad.code:
// "This looks slow."
const cachedNormalizeUsers = memoize(normalizeUsers);

rules.rationale: Without evidence, optimization effort often targets code that is not responsible for meaningful user-visible cost.
rules.summary: Use profiling, benchmarks, production telemetry, or a known complexity bound before sacrificing clarity for small performance gains.
rules.title: Measure before micro-optimizing

bad.code:
const total = rows
  .filter(isBillable)
  .map(getAmount)
  .reduce((sum, amount) => sum + amount, 0);

exceptions: For small collections or non-hot paths, a readable map/filter chain may be the better engineering choice.
rules.rationale: Repeated passes and intermediate allocations scale with dataset size and can become significant in data-heavy applications.
rules.summary: When processing large collections in a hot path, avoid chains that create avoidable intermediate arrays when one clear pass can do the work.
rules.title: Prefer one pass on hot large-data paths

rules.rationale: An appropriate data structure can remove repeated linear scans and communicate the intended operations directly.
rules.summary: Use arrays, sets, maps, indexes, or other structures according to how the data is actually queried and updated.
rules.title: Choose data structures for access patterns

rules.rationale: Separating presentation from behavior keeps components readable and makes logic independently testable.
rules.summary: Move substantial transformation, orchestration, and business logic out of component markup.
rules.title: Keep components focused on presentation

bad.code: const fullName = useMemo(() => `${firstName} ${lastName}`, [firstName, lastName]);

good.code: const fullName = `${firstName} ${lastName}`;

rules.rationale: Unnecessary memoization adds dependency management and cognitive overhead without guaranteed benefit.
rules.summary: Use memoization when identity matters or profiling demonstrates a meaningful benefit.
rules.title: Do not memoize by reflex

bad.code:
// Global store for state owned by one component
const modalStore = createStore({ isOpen: false });

good.code: const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false);

rules.rationale: Global state hides dependencies. Local state and explicit data flow make ownership easier to understand.
rules.summary: Use explicit props and local state until multiple consumers genuinely require shared ownership.
rules.title: Keep state as local as practical

bad.code:
const [fullName, setFullName] = useState("");
useEffect(() => setFullName(`${first} ${last}`), [first, last]);

good.code: const fullName = `${first} ${last}`;

rules.rationale: Duplicated state creates synchronization paths and can briefly or permanently disagree with its source values.
rules.summary: If a value can be calculated from current props or state during render, derive it instead of synchronizing another state variable.
rules.title: Do not store derived state

rules.rationale: Effects run after render and introduce a second execution phase. Keeping synchronous logic in render or event handlers reduces timing bugs.

references.label: React — You Might Not Need an Effect

rules.summary: Do not reach for useEffect for synchronous derivation or event handling that can happen directly.
rules.title: Use effects to synchronize external systems

bad.code: items.map((item, index) => <Row key={index} item={item} />)

exceptions: An index key is acceptable for a truly static list whose ordering and membership can never change.

good.code: items.map((item) => <Row key={item.id} item={item} />)

rules.rationale: Unstable keys can preserve state on the wrong item or force unnecessary unmounts and remounts.
rules.summary: Keys should identify the same logical item across inserts, deletes, sorting, and re-rendering.
rules.title: Use stable list keys

rules.rationale: React may render more than once, interrupt rendering, or discard work. Render-time side effects become unpredictable under those semantics.
rules.summary: Rendering should calculate UI from current inputs without mutating external state or causing observable side effects.
rules.title: Keep render pure

good.code:
const countryOptions = ["Canada", "France", "Japan"];

const CountrySelect = () => <Select options={countryOptions} />;

rules.rationale: Module-scope values communicate that they are invariant and avoid recreating objects or arrays on every render.
rules.summary: Constants and configuration that never depend on props or state should live at module scope.
rules.title: Move static values out of components

rules.rationale: React relies on stable Hook call order to associate state and effects with the correct component instance.
rules.summary: Call Hooks only at the top level of React components or custom Hooks, never inside loops, conditions, nested functions, or try/catch blocks.
rules.title: Follow the Rules of Hooks

bad.code: const UserCard = ({ user }) => {user.name}; const content = UserCard({ user });

good.code: const content = <UserCard user={user} />;

rules.rationale: React must control component invocation to preserve Hook behavior, reconciliation, and component identity.
rules.summary: Render components through JSX instead of invoking component functions directly.
rules.title: Let React call components

rules.rationale: React assumes render inputs remain stable for the duration of a render so it can restart, reuse, and optimize work safely.

references.label: React — Components and Hooks must be pure

rules.summary: Do not mutate values supplied by React or values already passed into Hooks or JSX.
rules.title: Treat props, state, and Hook inputs as immutable snapshots

rules.rationale: Missing dependencies make Effects and memoized callbacks observe outdated values and create timing-sensitive bugs.
rules.summary: Include the reactive values a Hook depends on instead of silencing exhaustive-dependency checks to preserve an intended stale closure.
rules.title: Do not suppress Hook dependency correctness

good.note: Split by coherent responsibility, not because a file crossed an arbitrary line count.

rules.rationale: Small focused units are easier to test and understand, but mechanical file-size limits often create fragmentation without improving cohesion.
rules.summary: Split a component or custom Hook when it owns multiple independent responsibilities or becomes difficult to scan, not merely because it crossed a fixed LOC threshold.
rules.title: Extract coherent React responsibilities, not arbitrary line counts

rules.rationale: Redux Toolkit is the official recommended toolset and encodes safer defaults for immutable updates, DevTools, and store configuration.
rules.summary: Prefer configureStore, createSlice, createAsyncThunk, RTK Query, and other Redux Toolkit APIs over hand-written legacy Redux boilerplate.
rules.title: Use Redux Toolkit for modern Redux

rules.rationale: Redux may replay reducer logic for debugging and hot reload; deterministic pure reducers make state transitions reproducible.
rules.summary: Reducers must not perform async work, generate nondeterministic values, mutate external variables, or trigger side effects.
rules.title: Keep reducers pure

exceptions: Middleware may intentionally intercept a non-serializable action before it reaches reducers.
rules.rationale: Serializable data preserves DevTools, persistence, replay, predictable equality behavior, and debugging.
rules.summary: Avoid Promises, functions, class instances, Maps/Sets, DOM nodes, and other non-serializable values in Redux state or actions that reach reducers.
rules.title: Keep Redux state and normal actions serializable

rules.rationale: Duplicated derived state introduces synchronization bugs and makes updates more complicated than recalculating from the source.
rules.summary: Store canonical source data and derive filtered, aggregated, or presentation-ready values through selectors.
rules.title: Keep Redux state minimal and derive the rest

rules.rationale: Normalization makes entity lookup and single-item updates simpler and reduces duplicated nested copies of the same entity.
rules.summary: Store heavily relational or repeatedly updated entity data in a normalized shape, typically with createEntityAdapter.
rules.title: Normalize complex relational collections

rules.rationale: Selectors create a stable read boundary so state structure can change without rewriting every consumer.
rules.summary: Reusable consumers should ask selectors for domain values instead of spreading knowledge of deep store paths throughout the UI.
rules.title: Use selectors to encapsulate state shape

good.code: const selectUserName = (state) => state.user.name;

rules.rationale: Unnecessary selector memoization adds complexity without avoiding work, while derived arrays and expensive calculations can benefit substantially.
rules.summary: Do not wrap every direct state lookup in createSelector; reserve memoization for real derivation or stable-reference needs.
rules.title: Memoize selectors only when they derive expensive or referentially new values

bad.code:
<input
  value={name}
  onChange={(event) => dispatch(nameChanged(event.target.value))}
/>

good.code:
const [name, setName] = useState("");

<input value={name} onChange={(event) => setName(event.target.value)} />

rules.rationale: Local state keeps ownership close to the UI and avoids dispatching global actions for data that is neither shared nor cached.
rules.summary: Do not put temporary form edits, hover state, or component-local interaction state in Redux without a genuine cross-application ownership need.
rules.title: Keep transient UI and form state local by default

bad.code:
export const userStore = configureStore({ reducer: userReducer });
export const settingsStore = configureStore({ reducer: settingsReducer });

rules.rationale: A single store preserves one state graph, one dispatch pipeline, and predictable DevTools/debugging behavior.
rules.summary: A standard Redux application should have one configured store instance shared through the application boundary.
rules.title: Use one Redux store per application

bad.code:
src/
  actions/users.ts
  reducers/users.ts
  selectors/users.ts

good.code:
src/
  features/users/
    usersSlice.ts
    usersSelectors.ts

rules.rationale: Feature-oriented slices improve cohesion and make the code that changes together easier to find and maintain.
rules.summary: Keep a feature's reducer logic, actions, and selectors close together, typically in a Redux Toolkit slice, instead of separating the app into global actions/reducers folders.
rules.title: Organize Redux logic by feature

bad.code:
const fetchTodos = createAsyncThunk("todos/fetch", fetchTodosApi);

// Slice also tracks request status, cache lifetime, and refetch logic.

rules.rationale: RTK Query provides request deduplication, caching, loading state, invalidation, and generated hooks while following Redux's recommended architecture.
rules.summary: When Redux is already the application state platform, use RTK Query as the default server fetching and caching layer instead of hand-writing request/cache reducers.
rules.title: Prefer RTK Query for server data in Redux applications

rules.rationale: The query key is TanStack Query's cache identity and dependency list; omitting an input can return or overwrite data under the wrong cache entry.
rules.summary: If the query function changes its result based on a variable, include that variable in the query key.
rules.title: Put every query dependency in the query key

bad.code: const queryKey = ["todos", () => status];

good.code: const queryKey = ["todos", { page, status }];

rules.rationale: TanStack Query hashes query keys to identify cached results; unstable or non-serializable identity makes caching unpredictable.
rules.summary: Use stable serializable values that uniquely describe the requested server data.
rules.title: Keep query keys serializable and deterministic

rules.rationale: TanStack Query considers cached data stale by default and refetches stale queries at useful lifecycle points; staleTime is the primary control for expected freshness.
rules.summary: Understand staleTime and the default refetch triggers before disabling mount, focus, or reconnect refetching globally.
rules.title: Configure freshness instead of fighting refetch behavior

rules.rationale: Targeted invalidation lets TanStack Query mark dependent data stale and refetch active consumers without manually synchronizing duplicate server state.
rules.summary: When a mutation makes cached server data stale, invalidate the smallest relevant query-key scope after success.
rules.title: Invalidate related queries after successful mutations

rules.rationale: TanStack Query determines error state from rejected query functions. Returning an error response as successful data bypasses retry and error handling.
rules.summary: A query function must throw or return a rejected Promise for failures; clients such as fetch need an explicit non-OK response check.
rules.title: Make query functions reject failed requests

bad.code:
openModal();
expect(modalController.state.isOpen).toBe(true);

good.code:
openModal();
expect(screen.getByRole("dialog")).toBeVisible();

rules.rationale: Behavior-focused tests survive safe refactors and fail when user-visible or contract-visible behavior actually changes.
rules.summary: Tests should verify a unit's public responsibility rather than reproduce its internal implementation.
rules.title: Test observable behavior

bad.code: expect(formatUser(null as never)).toBe("Unknown");

rules.rationale: Tests for impossible states add maintenance cost while distracting from failures the system can actually encounter.
rules.summary: Edge cases should come from real contracts and failure modes rather than impossible values invented only to increase coverage.
rules.title: Test realistic states

rules.rationale: Complex mocks duplicate behavior, drift from reality, and can make tests pass against a fake system that production never runs.
rules.summary: Replace external collaborators with the smallest useful test double instead of recreating the library or service inside the test.
rules.title: Mock the boundary, not its implementation

bad.code:
render(<Checkout subtotal={100} tier="gold" />);
expect(screen.getByText("$90.00")).toBeVisible();

rules.rationale: Direct tests are faster, clearer about failures, and avoid coupling business assertions to unrelated rendering or infrastructure.
rules.summary: When transformation or decision logic has its own responsibility, test it at that boundary rather than only through a distant UI or controller.
rules.title: Test pure logic directly

bad.code:
const { container } = render(<CheckoutPage />);
expect(container).toMatchSnapshot();

rules.rationale: Large snapshots are easy to approve mechanically and often obscure which behavior was intended to change.
rules.summary: Prefer focused assertions when the behavior can be expressed directly; use snapshots when a meaningful structured output is expensive to assert piecemeal.
rules.title: Use snapshots selectively

bad.code: expect(applyCoupon({ total: 100, expiresAt: tomorrow })).toBe(90);

rules.rationale: A regression test preserves the newly learned system constraint and prevents the same defect from silently returning.
rules.summary: When a bug can be reproduced deterministically, add a test that fails before the fix and passes after it.
rules.title: Protect fixed bugs with regression tests

bad.code: const buildParams = (params: any) => params;

exceptions: A tightly scoped third-party interoperability boundary may require a documented exception.
rules.rationale: any removes compiler guarantees at the boundary where they are most valuable and lets invalid states spread.
rules.summary: Use the narrowest correct type instead of opting out of type safety.
rules.title: Avoid any

bad.code: type Status = string;

good.code: type Status = "active" | "paused";

rules.rationale: Broad unions and unnecessary optional properties force consumers to handle states that cannot occur.
rules.summary: Model only states the runtime contract genuinely permits.
rules.title: Keep types narrow

bad.code:
import { User } from "./types";

const user: User = getUser();

good.code: import type { User } from "./types";

rules.rationale: Type-only imports communicate intent and prevent accidental runtime coupling or emitted imports.
rules.summary: Use import type when an import exists only in the type system.
rules.title: Use type-only imports

bad.code: const user = response.json() as User;

good.code:
const payload: unknown = await response.json();
const user = parseUser(payload);

rules.rationale: TypeScript types do not validate network responses, storage values, URL parameters, or other runtime input.
rules.summary: Parse and validate external data at a boundary before treating it as an internal domain type.
rules.title: Treat untrusted input as unknown

rules.rationale: Unnecessary optionality pushes null checks to every consumer and permits states the runtime contract may never produce.
rules.summary: Do not mark properties optional merely to satisfy existing call sites or silence type errors.
rules.title: Optional means genuinely optional

rules.rationale: Discriminated unions make invalid combinations unrepresentable and enable exhaustive handling.
rules.summary: When states have different valid fields, model them as explicit variants instead of combinations of unrelated booleans and optional properties.
rules.title: Model variants as discriminated unions

bad.code:
const user = payload as User;
renderUser(user);

exceptions: A narrow assertion is acceptable when runtime invariants are stronger than TypeScript can express and that invariant is documented or proven locally.
rules.rationale: Unchecked assertions can hide a real mismatch between the runtime contract and the type model.
rules.summary: Use narrowing, validation, or a more accurate type instead of asserting a value into the shape you wish it had.
rules.title: Do not cast to silence the compiler

bad.code:
git commit -am "Ship feature"
git push

good.code:
pnpm check
pnpm build

# Then commit and update the PR.

rules.rationale: Automated checks are cheaper and more consistent than asking reviewers to manually detect failures the toolchain already knows how to prove.
rules.summary: Type checking, linting, tests, build validation, generated artifacts, and other repository-specific checks should pass before code is merged.
rules.title: Run the relevant checks before merge

bad.code:
PR: Add CSV export
- Add CSV export
- Rename utils/ to shared/
- Replace the test runner
- Reformat unrelated files

good.code:
PR: Add CSV export
- Add CSV export
- Add export tests
- Update export documentation

rules.rationale: Focused diffs are easier to review, test, revert, and attribute when regressions occur.
rules.summary: Avoid mixing unrelated refactors, folder moves, migrations, cleanup, and behavior changes in one change unless the coupling is explicit and necessary.
rules.title: Keep changes scoped

bad.code: rm src/legacyParser.ts

good.code:
rg "legacyParser|parseLegacy" src tests config
# Inspect dynamic imports and generated/config wiring too.
rm src/legacyParser.ts

rules.rationale: Dead-code tools have blind spots around dynamic imports, reflection, configuration, and generated wiring; deleting live code is worse than temporarily keeping dead code.
rules.summary: Search static, dynamic, generated, and runtime entry points before concluding that code is unused.
rules.title: Verify usage before deleting code

bad.code:
## PR
Done.

good.code:
## PR
Adds the new parser.

Follow-up: #482 removes the legacy parser after migration.
Depends on: #479 landing first.

rules.rationale: Explicit follow-up boundaries prevent incomplete work from being mistaken for finished work and reduce accidental merge-order problems.
rules.summary: If tests, cleanup, migrations, or dependent changes intentionally land separately, make that dependency visible to reviewers.
rules.title: Call out deferred or dependent work
